clue.text: Rent, perhaps, around quarter in centre of city

indicators.note: to go around something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a renter, perhaps, is someone who doesn't own their home: DON'T OWN, apostrophe dropped
a quarter is a compass point; W is west

explanation.surface: Someone paying rent for a place in a central district of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like a noun for money paid, but here it describes what tenants do: they DON'T OWN. Slip the west point in after DO to get DOWNTOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiefly American usage for a city's central business district, the heart of town where shops and offices cluster.

clue.text: Part of ship that’s unaffected by overturning

indicators.note: a word that stays the same when flipped end to end reads identically in both directions

blocks.note: the raised deck at the stern of a ship; the definition doubles as the word to test, since a palindrome clue has nothing else to turn

explanation.surface: A piece of a vessel that stays put even if the boat capsizes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overturning' suggests a capsized ship, but it means reversing the word's letters; POOP reads the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The poop deck is the raised rear deck of an old sailing vessel, so it is one section of the hull's structure.

clue.text: Sally’s kind, in other words

blocks.note: a kind is a sort or type
i.e. abbreviates Latin id est, 'that is', used to rephrase

explanation.surface: Describing a woman called Sally as kind, to put it another way.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally is not a woman's name here but a military term, and the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden attack by troops breaking out from a besieged position, which is exactly a sortie.

clue.text: Minor ways in which Fourth of July is captured by women in US

indicators.note: asks for the letter in fourth position of the following word
something captured is held inside its captor, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: broads is American slang for women
fourth letter of the month's name

explanation.surface: Small-town American streets where women take part in Independence Day celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fourth of July' reads as the US holiday, but it only supplies the fourth letter of July. 'Broads' is dated American slang for women.
explanation.definitionFit: Byroads are secondary or side roads, less important routes away from main highways, so they are lesser roads.

clue.text: Plenty of power in short book, securing upturn of payment

indicators.note: in a down clue turning something upward makes it read from bottom to top
to secure is to hold firmly, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: Matt is a shortened form of Matthew, a book of the New Testament
a wage is a payment for work

explanation.surface: A concise book packed with energy, thanks to a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upturn of payment' sounds like a pay rise, but it turns the wage upside down. The abbreviated gospel goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A megawatt is a unit of a million watts, a large amount of electrical output by everyday standards.

clue.text: Small points about attack – it’s unfair to blame them

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the plural noun

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
capes are headlands, points of land jutting into the sea
to go at someone is to attack them

explanation.surface: Minor objections to an offensive move, with a protest that the blame is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' suggests arguments, but it means headlands; GO AT sits inside CAPES after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Scapegoats are people made to carry the blame for others' faults, so faulting them is unjust.

clue.text: Utter a diatribe, repeating its beginning

indicators.note: to repeat something is to say it again, so a letter is written twice over

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the diatribe word, used an extra time
a diatribe is an angry tirade

explanation.surface: Deliver a tirade, saying its opening words twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like a verb meaning to speak, but it is the adjective meaning complete. The R of RANT appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are intensifying adjectives meaning complete or downright, as in arrant nonsense or utter nonsense.

clue.text: Ploy contrived by Dr. No that eliminates the competition

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the noun

indicators.note: something contrived is artificially arranged, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor
taken as written
letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A Bond villain's scheme to wipe out his rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr No is the James Bond villain, but here the doctor and the word split. Monopoly is also the board game, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A monopoly is exclusive control of a market by one supplier, so it shuts out any rival businesses.

clue.text: Muffed her cue that involves up to three other players

definitions.text: that involves up to three other players
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the name of a card game

indicators.note: muffing something means botching it, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actress fluffs her cue in a scene with up to three other actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests actors on stage, but they are card players.
explanation.definitionFit: Euchre is a trick-taking card game for two to four people, played chiefly in North America.

clue.text: Shoot and fracture

blocks.note: first meaning: take a photograph
second meaning: break suddenly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' suggests gunfire causing a fracture, but it means taking a photo. Snap is also a children's card game, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap is a quick photograph, and to snap is to break cleanly with a crack, as a bone or stick might.

clue.text: Retaliatory principle that applies to surrounding solutions

annotation.answer: TWO CAN PLAY AT THAT GAME

blocks.note: surface reading: a saying justifying paying someone back in kind
setter's reading: the neighbouring across entries are all games that can be played by a pair

explanation.surface: A tit-for-tat rule that somehow governs the answers around it.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is literally true of the theme: across answers like Monopoly, Scrabble, Snap and Draughts are games for two players.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns an opponent that you will answer their tactics in kind, a principle of tit-for-tat revenge.

clue.text: Be astounded finding trunk filled with goods?

indicators.note: something filled has contents placed inside it

blocks.note: a bole is the trunk of a tree
G stands for good, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Being amazed to discover a travel trunk crammed with merchandise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' suggests luggage, but it is a tree trunk. G for good is a common grading abbreviation. Boggle is also a word game, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: When the mind boggles it is overwhelmed with amazement, unable to take something in.

clue.text: Firm, for instance, set up painful new version of hide-and-seek?

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: CO is short for company, a firm
e.g. means for example
aching means sore or painful

explanation.surface: A company launching a painful updated take on a children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' suggests a company establishing something, but it flips the company and example abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Geocaching is a modern outdoor pastime of hiding containers and finding them using GPS coordinates, a high-tech treasure hunt.

clue.text: Swallows in air currents

blocks.note: first meaning: gulps of drink
second meaning: cold streams of air in a room

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures birds riding the wind, but swallows are mouthfuls of drink. Draughts is the British name for checkers, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught is a single gulp of liquid, and also a current of cool air blowing through a gap.

clue.text: Place for mate, in more ways than one

definitions.text: Place for mate, in more ways than one

blocks.note: surface reading: where a ship's officer or a companion belongs
setter's reading: checkmate happens on a chessboard, and a ship's mate serves aboard a vessel

explanation.walkthrough: Mate is both the chess finish and a ship's officer; both are found in the same spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Checkmate is delivered on the chessboard, while a ship's first mate works aboard the vessel.

clue.text: Replace workers in advance, putting boot dreadfully in

indicators.note: something done dreadfully is done badly, so the letters end up out of order
putting something in places it inside another piece

blocks.note: letters rearranged
a rise is an advance or increase

explanation.surface: Sacking staff ahead of time, cruelly putting the boot in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In advance' reads as 'beforehand', but advance is RISE, and the jumbled boot goes in it.
explanation.definitionFit: To robotise is to automate a job so that machines take over tasks once done by human staff.

clue.text: Location for people holding hands and eating

definitions.text: Location for people holding hands and eating

blocks.note: surface reading: a spot where people link hands, perhaps couples or a seance
setter's reading: card players hold hands of cards, and diners sit to eat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding hands' suggests affection, but a hand is a set of playing cards; card players and diners both sit in the same spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Both card games and meals take place with people seated around a raised flat piece of furniture.

clue.text: Flies part of journey in pants

indicators.note: a piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: longs are long trousers, which Americans call pants
a leg is one stage of a journey

explanation.surface: Insects get in someone's trousers partway through a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' could be a verb about air travel or the zip on trousers, but it is the insects: daddy-long-legs, or crane flies.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-legs is a name for the crane fly, the thin gangly insect also called daddy-long-legs.

clue.text: Gag about mother’s chance to get even

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: to gag is to retch
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A joke about Mum's opportunity for revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke, but it is the verb meaning to heave; the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rematch is a second contest that lets the loser of the first try to level the score.

clue.text: Caught in small mob, use claws

indicators.note: a piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
S is the abbreviation for small
a rabble is a disorderly mob

explanation.surface: Trapped in a little crowd, someone fights with their nails.
explanation.walkthrough: The catch goes between the small S and the mob. Scrabble is also the word game, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrabble is to scratch or grope about frantically with the fingers or claws.

clue.text: Boat in sea – in sound, say

indicators.note: taking a word by how it is pronounced rather than spelt

blocks.note: the letter name C is pronounced like the word sea
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: A vessel out at sea, perhaps in a strait or channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like a body of water to go with sea, but it signals the letter that is pronounced like sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutter is a small fast single-masted sailing vessel, also used for patrol craft.

clue.text: A coin’s tossed in gambling scene

indicators.note: something tossed is thrown about, so these letters land in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone flips a coin while betting.
explanation.walkthrough: Casino is also the name of a card game, part of the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino is a venue where people bet money on cards, dice and roulette wheels.

clue.text: Service provider moved around in circle

indicators.note: letters moved around are shifted into a different order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A utility firm's engineer travels a circular route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service provider' sounds like a utility or internet company, but the service is a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric is a member of the clergy, who leads religious worship such as church services.

clue.text: See 11
What follows foxtrot on radio brings beat back

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction, right to left

blocks.note: to flog is to beat

explanation.surface: A radio station plays a foxtrot dance tune that brings back an old rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: Foxtrot reads as a dance, but it is F in the radio alphabet (Alpha, Bravo...), which is followed by Golf for G.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet used in radio communication, the code word after Foxtrot is Golf.

clue.text: Nasty remark greatly upset European

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so in a down clue it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: big, as in 'think big', means on a grand scale
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A cruel comment deeply hurt someone from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greatly upset' reads as 'very distressed', but greatly gives BIG and upset flips it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibe is a taunting or mocking comment intended to hurt, so it is an insult.

clue.text: Activity in court that makes offence clear? Just the opposite

indicators.note: the opposite order puts the whole string back to front

blocks.note: a sin is an offence
to net is to clear as profit after deductions

explanation.surface: A courtroom procedure that clarifies a crime, or perhaps the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court. 'Just the opposite' tells you to read the offence-then-clear string backwards rather than as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is a racket sport played on a court, so it is a sporting pastime played there.

clue.text: Copy book ahead of time as popular local activity

definitions.note: 'local' is British slang for a pub

blocks.note: to crib is to copy someone else's work
B is the abbreviation for book
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Reserving early for a well-liked community event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copy book' suggests a schoolbook, and 'book ahead' suggests reserving; in Britain a 'local' is one's neighbourhood pub, where cribbage is traditionally played.
explanation.definitionFit: Cribbage is a card game scored with pegs on a board, long a fixture of British pub life.
